cards.title: Don't couple your Go code to GitHub

depth.text: someone says Go packages should use **custom domains** so changing code hosts won't mean rewriting **import paths**

Go uses the hosting location in an **import path**, so moving hosts can mean changing code. The author recommends a custom domain that can point somewhere new while users keep the **same install command**. One company used GitHub, GitLab and Azure Devops at once because switching was such a large task, and ended up paying for **three hosting services**.

cards.camps: Two camps: custom-domain advocates say they avoid tying package names to one host; critics say domains need upkeep and can disappear, while some say a go.mod replace or find-and-replace is enough.

comments.text: True, but beware of the domain name you're using. Because VeriSign may unilaterally decide to delete your domain name along with thousands of others [1] and you're back to square one… [1] https://neil.fraser.name/news/2026/09/03/

> In my opinion, every commerical software development team using Go should be using custom domains for namespacing their internal libraries and packages. I’d remove “go” from the above, i.e. I think same applies to other stacks. Even using GitHub domain links in code comments gets problematic long term. Ie when a migration happens and those links start pointing nowhere.

> That is, if you move your git hosting to GitLab then you have to change your code! You can also just use "replace github.com/example/example => gitlab.com/example/example" in your go.mod file and everything will keep working. That seems like a very pre-mature optimization for something that doesn't really matter.

> One of the good features of Go is that you namespace your code with the location to fetch the code. Then the rest of the article explains why this is NOT a good feature in practice. I don't think it's unworkable either, but this is one of these little thing that Go decided to do different and convinced its fans that this is a great idea and all the other languages where doing it wrong. After a…

You will never be as good as Microsoft to keep paying for the domain. There are no guarantees in life but I…

cards.title: Self-Hosting on the Dark Web

depth.text: someone made their **personal site** reachable on **Tor**, with a separate build for its onion address

The **.onion address** works only inside Tor; Tor forwards its port 80 to **nginx**, listening at 127.0.0.1:8080. The author uses **Hugo** to build separate clearnet and Tor copies, then deploys both on every push.

cards.camps: Two camps: the post says Tor keeps any single party from linking identity to activity; one commenter says government agencies can still do it, just with more difficulty.

comments.text: My personal website has been hosted on Tor for years. It's easy to do from your home even behind a NAT because it's an outgoing connection from your point of view (which also makes it a great way to expose local services even when you are behind a NAT and don't not have a static IP), and by design your personal IP is hidden from your visitors. I wrote about it in 2600 almost ten years ago…

What I really love about Onion sites is that if they are big enough, performance engineering really becomes Tor-specific. A few examples: - Making assets embedded as base64 (img src the header logo as base64, all CSS should be inline, etc.). - Leveraging CSS as much as possible (if you use animations and transitions, use CSS as much as possible for these, avoid JS for them). - Make sure your…
You probably want to add the Onion-Location header to the clearnet site so Tor Browser can automatically inform the visitor about it: https://community.torproject.org/onion-services/advanced/oni...

Besides using a separate port, I would also suggest running the hidden service on a non-127.0.0.1 bind address, just in case you ever host something else on that port and forget to disable the hidden service: > HiddenServicePort 80 127.13.37.1:8080 > listen 127.13.37.1:8080; This way, strangers won't be able to connect to a service bound to 127.0.0.1, should you ever decide to re-use the port and…
What is the benefit of building the same website twice with different hostnames instead of using relative links to content on the same domain?

cards.title: Writing Efficient C++ Code (2013)

depth.text: someone explains why **keeping data together** can help C++ code **run faster**

The article's **Data-Oriented Design** advice is to plan where data sits in memory before choosing algorithms; scattered, pointer-linked objects can cause **cache misses**. It also reports a two-line change that saved **25%** of execution time.

cards.camps: Two camps: one says contiguous data can beat pointer-heavy structures in practice; the other says performance gains are often negligible and the code just gets more complex.

comments.text: This article reminds me of performance advice I was starting to see in the 2000s decade. Basically it was to not introduce a bunch of pointer heavy data structures to get lower algorithmic complexity. Stuff it all into a vector. You will use some algorithms that the computer science textbook will say it's slower, but if it fits all in cache it doesn't matter. The cache misses following pointers…

While we're here, has anyone seen any resources related to data-oriented design when GCs are involved? So much of data-oriented design is arena-focused, but that's not always possible, when the lifetime model of the code requires a GC (for whatever reason). I feel like the DoD movement is a slow-moving, but big, change through how systems programming is done, but that there's still insufficient…

There's no mention of branch prediction, or context switching, or synchronisation. Depending on what you're doing, they could be very consequential. There's only very brief mention of parallelisation with threads and with SIMD. High-performance programming is a big topic. The scope is far too broad for a single blog post, which naturally gives only cursory discussion of C++ and computer…
I write in C++ almost every day but never have the need to optimize for speed. Even when you write straightforward code it's already blazingly fast.

A few weeks back there was this nice little database query language as a language library [1] posted on HN, with the constraint that everything had to be 6NF. At the time I thought this would naturally fit in a data-oriented design/ECS system to run complex queries. I wonder whether anyone has tried this before and whether this actually works in practice? [1] https://prela-lang.org/tutorial/

cards.title: Alan Kay's answer to “Did the ENIAC have a BIOS”?

depth.text: Commenters say Alan Kay treated the **people with patch cables** as ENIAC's **BIOS**

One commenter says the original ENIAC had to be **physically reconfigured**, then was rebuilt to run as a **stored-program computer** from '48 to '55. Another argues BIOS wasn't a concept until **1975**, with CP/M.

cards.camps: Two camps: some use “BIOS” as a metaphor for the people operating ENIAC; another says it couldn't have had a BIOS because the concept came later.

comments.text: EDSAC as early as 1949 had an "initial orders" module. A boot-up ROM. There was a bank of rotary selector switches, to set the octal digits in each ROM word. David Wheeler (of subroutine fame) figured out the most sensible thing to put in the tiny ROM was a paper tape loader and mini-assembler that loaded the rest of itself from paper tape. So at switch-on the machine would start reading the tape…

Somewhat tangential, I've watched a bunch of videos on YouTube from @deramp5113 about the Altair 8800 and other early microcomputers, which feature a similar set of front panel switches for dialing in your initial program. One thing that's interesting to me, as someone who learned computing in the late 90s, is how much is expressed in octal instead of hex on these early computers. As shown in the…

I had Claude Opus disassemble the CDC 6600 dead start panel. The hard part was finding a better image of the switches so the vision could read the bits.¹ The content isn't very interesting, and Claude's comments aren't very detailed. Not bad for 2 minutes of work about a 62 year old computer though. Look out Ken Shirriff, AI is coming for you.² Addr Octal Instruction Meaning
0001 7512 DCN 12…

I'm pretty sure Kay's not quite correct about the Eniac not being a stored program computer. In it's original form it obviously was not, as it had to physically reconfigured to solve different problems. However, after the war it was rebuilt to operate like any other stored program (von Neumann architecture) computer, as it was the first recipient of the design philosophy seen in the EDVAC report…
How often would those cold-start switches be altered? Just when they wanted to swap tape-reading hardware? Or did different programs want slightly different loaders?

cards.title: There is more to code review than (automatable) detection

depth.text: someone argues **code review** does more than catch bugs, because people bring **context, judgment and accountability**

The essay says agents can perform code review’s stated functions, but argues that treating review as detection misses the **context** people carry from outside the codebase. It calls review **coordination**, sensemaking and governance too.

cards.camps: Two camps: human-review defenders say people catch missing context, teach teammates and provide accountability; others argue human review can’t keep pace with AI-generated code and should shift toward design or broader validation.
entities: The End of Code Review: Coding Agents Supersede Human Inspection

At the end, if taken seriously, at least two people understand how the feature works (even if that number is, on average, trending closer to between one and zero). Ideally at least one of the two also comes away with a better…

cards.title: Parley: Federated, decentralised chat that speaks plain IRC

depth.text: someone built a **chat network** where people run their own **instances** and use regular **chat clients**

Parley uses **email-like identities**, so people can message someone on another instance with an address like alice@foo.com. It’s a **working proof of concept**, and the project says it is **not hardened yet**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters compare it to XMPP or ask why it isn't built on an existing network; others like the idea and call it email for IM.

comments.text: There’s a specific downside to LLM-based development that people can get neck deep in a new project without interfacing with the existing work in the field. In this case, this is basically a poorly specified implementation of half of XMPP. Of course, I half expect the LLM would have mentioned that at some point, but the repository does not.
How do you plan to handle bad actors creating biblical amounts of servers dynamically and then spamming at line rate from all of those servers?
So rooms are "global" between whatever hosts your host happens to know about? So it's one giant netsplit party forever and only your server admin can ban someone?

Instead of a separate federated network for a single app, why not implement the app on top of a pre-existing federated network, so that nobody has to create yet another account?
Like, on top of atproto or activitypods or...?

Interesting. Why not use an open link network? These will result in around the same state. Spam _will_ be an issue here, in general. And with a different backend you're going to struggle to use preexisting tooling to handle it. Using & channels is fun, I'd be interested to see how many bots and clients fall over dead when faced with that particular bit of IRC history.

glossary.stock options: A deal that gives someone the right to buy company shares later at an agreed price.

glossary.stock split: A company divides each share into more shares, with each one representing a smaller part of the company.
glossary.statute of limitations: A legal deadline for starting a case about something that happened.
glossary.motion to dismiss: A request asking a judge to end a case before it goes to trial.
glossary.pixel art: Pictures built from visible colored squares, often with a blocky look.
glossary.Web Audio API: A set of tools built into browsers for making and controlling sound.
glossary.sound synthesis: Making sounds electronically instead of playing recorded audio.
glossary.import path: The address Go uses to identify and fetch a package.
glossary.Go vanity URL: A custom web address that lets a Go package keep the same name even if its code host changes.
glossary.go.mod: A project file that tells Go which other packages it depends on.
glossary.301 redirect: A web instruction that permanently sends someone from one address to another.

glossary.range voting: A way to choose by letting each voter give options scores, then comparing those scores.
glossary.trademark: A name or logo legally protected so people can tell whose product or project it is.

glossary.desoldering pump: A hand tool that sucks melted solder off a connection so a part can come loose.
glossary.LIR2477: A battery code; commenters say the R marks a rechargeable cell and 77 gives its height in tenths of a millimetre.
glossary.battery chemistry: The kind of materials inside a battery, which affects how it works and what charger it needs.
glossary.voltage: A measure of the electrical push a battery provides.

glossary.rsync: A tool for copying files between folders or machines and keeping them in sync.
glossary.suborbital: A flight that goes high into space but does not circle Earth.
glossary.splashdown: A spacecraft landing in water instead of on land.
glossary.critical path: The chain of jobs that must finish in order before a project can be done.
glossary.LEO: Low Earth orbit: a region fairly close to Earth where satellites travel around the planet.
glossary.effort: A setting that controls how much the model thinks about its answer.
glossary.evals: Short tests used to check how well a model handles tasks you care about.
glossary.prompt injection: Instructions hidden in text or a file that try to trick an AI into ignoring its intended directions.
glossary.harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
glossary.prompt cache: A saved copy of earlier instructions that a system can reuse instead of handling them again.
glossary.Data-Oriented Design (DOD): A way to plan code by arranging its data first, then choosing how to work on it.
glossary.cache miss: When needed data isn't in the computer's small, fast holding area, so it must fetch it from slower memory.
glossary.Array of Structures (AOS): A layout where each item's different values, like its position and color, sit together.
glossary.Structure of Arrays (SOA): A layout that keeps all positions together, all colors together, and so on.
glossary.Q&A: Question and answer: a session where guests respond to questions.
glossary.hit piece: A story or film made mainly to attack someone, rather than give a fair account.
glossary.BIOS: Basic Input/Output System: the software that gets a computer ready to load its main programs.
glossary.stored-program computer: A computer that keeps its instructions in memory instead of needing its hardware rewired for each job.
glossary.octal: A way to write numbers using eight digits, from 0 through 7.
glossary.bootloader: A small program that starts a computer and loads its main software.
glossary.diff: A view showing what changed between two versions of code.
glossary.PR: Pull request: a proposed code change shared so others can review it.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.absence blindness: A tendency to miss something that should be there but isn’t.
glossary.sensemaking: The work of figuring out what is happening and what it means.
glossary.federated: A setup where separate services can communicate instead of everyone needing to use one central service.
glossary.instance: One separately run copy of a service, with its own operator and users.
glossary.IRC: Internet Relay Chat: a way to chat live with people in online rooms.
glossary.DNS: Domain Name System: the internet's address book, which helps a computer find a website from its name.
glossary.XMPP: Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol: a way for messaging apps to exchange messages.
